“Do you want to tell the story?” Bill North, professor of Medieval History at Carleton, asked his wife, colleague and office neighbor, Victoria Morse.

“Well, we can both tell it,” said Morse. According to her, the history department position that the two now hold was advertised as a position for a single medieval historian. “So we contacted the department and said, ‘Well actually, there are two of us, would you consider splitting it?”

While faculty and staff are often seen only in their professional roles, many have built lives deeply intertwined with the institution and each other. These four relationships spanning different departments and stages of life give us a glimpse into another side of professors, administrators and coaches, as well as another aspect of the Carleton community. 

North clarifies that he and Morse had applied to the same position separately but informed the history department that they were married and interested in living and working in the same place. “We would be open to whatever possibilities there were,” North said.

“We would consider splitting [the position] if the department was open to it. And they were,” Morse said. In 1999, she and North moved into office 203B in Leighton Hall together, the same room Morse still works out of today.

“At a certain point, the college decided that we could each have an office,” she said. “And we took these two because we liked the idea that we are right next door to the other half of our book collection,” Morse said as she gestured to the shelves in North’s room that covered the wall separating their office.

“It’s very handy to think of it as just one big office, but with a wall,” said Morse.

While the couple shared a workspace, books and position, North says the college did not “treat us like half a researcher.” Each was given their own computer and faculty research account. “They treated us very much as discrete people, but the teaching load was divided.”

The couple had their daughter during their first year at Carleton. In those years, North says they called themselves the “morning medievalist” and the “afternoon medievalist.”

Recalling the times they split the work day between them, Morse said, “We used to joke that the department could be reassured that there was a medieval historian on duty at all times, and that their medieval history needs would be met, AM or PM.”

As she spoke, North launched into a brief monologue: “We have a medieval emergency; where is the relevant professional? But I don’t need an early Modernist! THIS IS A MEDIEVAL PROBLEM!”

“Strangely enough, we don’t have that many people knocking on our door with medieval history emergencies. But we are always holding ourselves in readiness,” Morse said.

More than two decades since their arrival in Northfield, Kristen Vogel, assistant director of the writing center, describes North and Morse as an institution of their own. “They’re such a powerhouse here,” said Vogel.

While North and Morse met at a departmental gathering as graduate students in the UC Berkeley History department, Kristen Vogel and her husband, Schuyler Vogel ’07, the College Chaplain, took a more modern technology-driven approach: the couple came across one another’s profiles on Tinder. At the time, she was teaching at a university in Milwaukee while he was working at a congregation in the suburbs.

According to Kristen Vogel, “Something that I really remembered about his dating profile was he was holding a baby duck in one of his pictures.” The duckling won a favorable reaction from her: “I was like, ‘love that.’”

She said Schuyler’s personality lines up with the picture, “He’s a nurturing guy, he’s a gentle guy, which I love.”

Not long after meeting in Milwaukee, he got a job in New York City, and the couple moved there. “That was kind of a leap,” said Kristen Vogel, “but worth it in the end.” “I was like, if it doesn’t work out, I’m in New York, and it’s cool.”

“Because I was thinking I might go teach in Spain, and I was all ready to do that. Then I met him, and I was like, darn it.” Kristen Vogel said she decided to move to New York with him after asking, “If I go to Spain, what would you do?”

According to Kristen Vogel, he replied, “we’ll make it work…I needed to know that it wasn’t just me doing it, me making a sacrifice,” she said.

The couple moved to Northfield in 2023 when Schuyler Vogel got the job as Chaplain. He says he had worked in the Chapel as a student at Carleton. “And so I’d always thought about this position because the chaplain during my time was pretty influential to me, and I was like, well, maybe when she retires one day, I’ll just throw my hat in the ring.”

However, Carolyn Fure-Slocum ’82, the chaplain who preceded Schuyler Vogel, “just didn’t retire for a very, very long time. She was here for 27 years.” When she did retire, however, he applied for the job, and “was fortunate to be offered the position.”

On a more personal note, Schuyler Vogel said, “I think Kristen was as interested in returning to the Midwest. We thought it might be a nice move for our family.”

In Kristen Vogel’s own words, “I was excited to move, though. We were both gunning for him to get that job. We were just ready to leave New York.”

“I love New York City,” said Kristen Vogel. But after having their first son, “we were like,’ we’re never gonna be able to own property in this city.’ It’s just not happening and it’s super expensive and it’s a very different lifestyle.”

She continued, “We felt like we needed more space; we wanted to settle down more,” and the couple chose Northfield as the place to do just that.

The Vogels’ kids are in daycare with the son of Ryan Terrien ’09 and Amanda Hund ’10. “There’s a healthy population of Carleton babies and kids,” said Terrien. Terrian, Associate Professor of Physics and Astronomy, and Hund, Assistant Professor of Biology, are both Carleton alumni.

The couple met in a scuba diving class while they were students. “It was one of these weird, occasional PE classes.” Terrien took the class because there was a chance he would be going to Florida for graduate school. He said, in his recollection, Hund took the class in preparation for the Australia Off-Campus Study program, “so she had maybe better justification.”

After graduating, Terrien attended graduate school at Penn State. When Hund graduated a year later, she moved to Pennsylvania too. “In addition to being a very talented scientist, [Amanda] was a very talented equestrian,” said Terrien. “So she was a working student at a barn there for a while and trained horses and did a bunch of work for a guy that was in the Olympics over and over. So she’s got talents.”

After her time in Pennsylvania, Hund moved to Colorado for graduate school. According to Terrian, in those years, the two were “spending all our money on plane tickets.”

After receiving his doctorate, Terrian moved to Colorado to work as a post-doc while Hund finished her degree. Then the two moved to Minnesota when Terrien was hired at Carleton. After some time as a researcher at the University of Minnesota, Hund also ended up at Carleton. However, Terrien said this is not a result they could have planned for.

As academics, “you pretty quickly learn that you don’t have a whole lot of choice about where you work…But the gravity was definitely pulling here,” he said. 

Cathy Carlson, associate Dean of Students, said she did not know Terrian and Hund were married. “I work with both of them, but I didn’t know they were together.” However, Cathy Carlson and her husband, Bob Carlson, a professor of Physical Education, Athletics and Recreation (PEAR) and head coach of men’s soccer, are yet another cross-department couple that is of surprise to some students.

According to Cathy Carlson, students sometimes tell her, “I’m taking Bob Carlson’s soccer course.” She waits to reveal their relationship because “I want them to be able to say what they’d like to say about Bob’s class.” When the information is revealed, however, “they almost always lean back in their chair and just go, ‘Oh, really? Oh my gosh,’” she said. “It is very, very funny.”

Bob Carlson said their relationship has been successful because their values match, and these values translate into the work we do. “I think Cathy is so gifted at working with students. We have different ways of working with students, but I think we’ll share the value of education.” “[We] share an enthusiasm for working with students, and watching them grow, and develop and thrive in a place like Carleton,” he said.
